caption_en: 40. Triclinium (e), S wall, detail of the upper area: horizontal zigzag border, upper part of the candelabrum stem and floating green garland. IV style.

41. Cubicle (h): cocciopesto floor with opus sectile emblem consisting of square tiles placed at each corner and triangular tiles of polychrome marbles (Lunense, Numidian); the border is black and white mosaic with a motif of triangles with overlapping concave sides; The border of cocciopesto has an ornament outlined in white tesserae: swastika meanders alternating with squares and squares with concave sides inscribed within circles. Mid-first century A.D. Diap. AlFreiburg (Fot. W. Gut)

42. Cubicle (h), N wall: the gaps highlight the oldest IV style decoration, with a scheme corresponding to that of the original IV style painting of the S. Red plinth wall with tufts, separated from the middle area by a white ornamental band. Yellow midway with slight architectural
43. Cubicle (h), N wall, middle area: detail of the central architecture with candelabra. IV style.
44. Cubicle (h), N wall, middle zone: floating cupid with cornucopia. IV style.

45. Cubicle (h), wall E, with door to the atrium (b). Oldest decoration in the fourth style: yellow plinth; Middle area: white compartment with candelabra and yellow side panel with vignette. The fresco is tapped by the superimposition of a second plaster. IV style.
46. Cubicle (h), wall E, oldest decoration in the fourth style: detail of the vignette with a two-wheeled cart pulled by two goats, on which there are tools.

47. Cubicle (h), wall S: plinth and middle area with more recent painting in the fourth style, corresponding to the decoration of wall N. The upper area has been lost and the gap has brought to light the original decoration in the fourth style: white compartment with candelabrum and two-tone side panel (white and yellow) divided by candelabra, with mystical cyst; Rotated ribbon carpet edges, running wave carpet edges and hanging lyra. IV style.
48. Cubicle (h), S wall, upper area: oldest decoration. IV style.
49. Cubicle (h), S wall, upper area: oldest decoration, right side with central architecture. IV style. Diap. AlFreiburg (Fot. W. Gut)

50. Stairwell (i) wall O: red plinth with shrubs and birds, separated from the black middle area by green stripes; middle area divided by dark red vertical stripes and white lines. At the height of the upper balcony, there is a black area divided into fields by red stripes and white lines, within which there are light green and red frames, connected to each other by golden sticks in an oblique position. Inside the frames, golden palmettes and a kantharos. On the central frame is a crouching sphinx. IV style.
51. Stairwell (i), wall O: red plinth, section S with tuft. IV style.
52. Stairwell (i), wall O: upper area with crouching sphinx. IV style.

53. Stairwell (i), wall E: red plinth; middle area with a black background divided into fields by white lines. In the upper area, the southern jamb of the large door of the atrium (b) covered with stucco, prior to the earthquake of 62 AD. C. IV style.

54. Tablinum (k), floor: emblem in opus sectile with square Numidian tiles inscribed within a rectangle formed by marble slabs; the emblem is further framed by black and white mosaic borders: a three-strand braid, a field of white tesserae and a border of staircase meanders alternating with squares; in section E there is a mat with two squares placed side by side inscribed within squares; step covered with marble on the S. side Mid-century A.D.

55. Tablinum (k), S wall, section E: plinth with a red background, with a three-sided frame of perforated borders with semicircles alternating with triangles; inside, Musa seated turned to the right. Middle area with a yellow background with a zigzag horizontal border filled with palmettes alternately upwards and downwards. IV style.

56. Garden (m), wall N: marble floor covering of the ventilation boxes inserted in the ground. In front of the N wall, a mosaic fountain with a tympanum roof. A black-bottomed plinth with a fence of oblique yellow reeds, bordered at the top by horizontal yellow stripes. Above, red frames of fake windows with shaded inner sides of the jambs and pediment coverings. In the center of the upper wall are golden shields with protomes of Medusa and red tapeworms. Thick garlands of green leaves are attached to the upper edges of the windows and to the outer cornices. In front of the central jamb is a golden candelabrum. Both windows open onto a view of the garden with oleanders and other bushes. In the window on the left is a sphinx; birds flying in the bushes and perched on basins are also represented. In the upper area figuni.
58. Garden (m), N wall, western window: the sphinx with open blue wings supports a golden fountain basin. IV style.

57. Garden (m), N wall, external W side of the fountain: pictorial decoration identical to that of the N wall of the garden. On the floor, a red channel. In the fountain basin, round masonry installation for water features. IV style.
59. Garden (m), N wall, window E: garland of large leaves, birds, golden shield with Medusa protome and tapeworms. IV style.

60. Garden (m), wall E, section N: decorative scheme similar to that of wall N, but with a single false window, with an arched roof, in the center of which is a golden helmet and a mask with long brown hair hanging from a golden chain. In the center of the window is a statue resting on a circular base. In the upper area, bush and tree with birds on the branches. IV style.
61. Garden (m), wall E, section N: arch covering the false window with golden helmet and mask. IV style. AlFreiburg (Fot. W. Gut)
62. Garden (m), wall E, section N: upper area, bush and tree. IV style.
63. Garden (m), wall E, section S: plinth with a red background with a frame of white perforated borders; inside, sea griffon vulture facing right. Diap. AlFreiburg (Fot. W. Gut)

64. Garden (m), wall E, section S: upper area with a yellow background with a coffered ceiling, from which a pinax hangs; below the pinax, bust of a bearded male figure; Thin garlands are attached to the upper corners of the pinax. IV style.

65. Garden (m), fountain: the front side of the basin has a pictorial decoration imitating cipollino marble; the aedicule is covered with polychrome glass mosaic: above a frieze with Poseidon among marine animals, in the apse basin is Aphrodite inside a shell; the piers of the aedicule are decorated with gorgoneìa in lozenges and the pendentives with cupids; in the tympanum that crowns the aedicule, there is a female figure ending in shoots; the plinth of the niche is treated as a pseudo-cave, with encrustations of pumice and shells, while the plinth of the piers is made of marble. Mid-first century A.D.
66. Tank, with lead pipe along the internal perimeter and sprayers for water features; the internal wall is rendered as a fake cave. In the frieze, part O is a water landscape and swans. IV style.
68. Pool, inner side, frieze, eastern part: water landscape, with coloured ducks and swan. IV style.
67. Pool, inner side, frieze, central part: water landscape, colored ducks, snake, frogs. IV style. Diap. AlFreiburg (Fot. W. Gut)

1. Vestibule (a), wall E: the decoration directed the gaze towards the interior of the house, alternating in the high plinth panels with carpet edges and narrow compartments with twisted candelabra. IV style.

2. Room (b), wall S: in consideration of the small size of the wall, the decoration scheme is divided into two parts by a narrow central compartment with a candelabra, on the sides of which are two panels with carpet edges. IV style.

3. Atrium (c): in the center of the room the impluvium, deeper than usual, may contain a bronze jet, which was hidden by a block of lava (still visible in the old photographs in Warsher, cited in bibl.), from which the water must have flowed. The edge of the pool is bordered by marble slabs within a strip of the same material. On the two short sides are the semicircular mouth of the cistern (in the foreground) and a small pillar, also covered with marble, which must have supported a fountain, in the masonry of which the water conduit was inserted. The bottom of the impluvium was also embellished with insertions of marble (Numidian) and stone tiles, now restored and reduced to a central rhombus and eight hexagonal tiles along the margins. On the right of the photograph, below the debris, there must be the tap to turn off the fountain supply, present in the old Warsher photographs.
4. Atrium (c): detail of the tiles preserved at the bottom of the impluvium. The marble manhole cover inserted on the S side (on the right in the photograph, in shadow) is also visible.

5. Atrium (c), NaE side of the room door (g): high plinth with red panel bordered by carpet edges. From Brizio (cited in bibl.) we know that the panels were adorned with 'griffins and neglected views of villages'. IV style.
6. Atrium (c), Entrance to the door side of the fauces (k) and the room (e): high red plinth with carpet edge panel. IV style.

7. Atrium (c), wall O: in this section the simple decoration of the room is better preserved, consisting of a plinth, higher than usual, with red panels divided by a narrow yellow compartment containing a twisted candelabrum. IV style.
8. Atrium (c), corner N-0: plinth with high red panel with carpet edges. IV style. 79 N52673
9. Room (e), wall N: simple decoration of the fourth style with a two-part scheme with a red plinth containing two large panels with plants and a white middle area.
10. Room (e), wall E: the collapse of the wall decoration of the IV style has brought out the fresco below, tapped to better adhere to the covering of the second phase.

11. Room (e), wall O: on this wall, better preserved, it is possible to read the simplicity of the decoration, which expands beyond the usual two-part scheme with a central compartment crossed by a candelabrum. The plinth is red, with panels with plants, the middle area white. IV style.

12. Room (g), N wall: remains of a fresco of the fourth style with a red plinth and a white middle area. The decoration of the room was extremely simple and Brizio (cited in bibl.) describes as the only ornaments 'griffins and vases enclosed in various compartments, the interstices of which must have been filled with landscapes, of which only one on the right is preserved'.
13. Room (g), wall E, section N: red plinth with panels with plants alternating with narrow compartments; White middle area: panels alternating with narrow compartments with candelabras.
14. Room (g), S side, opening towards the atrium (b) with jambs in limestone and tuff blocks; the decoration of the fourth style collapsed, leaving a tapped layer underneath.

15. Room (g): only wall O retains traces that are a little more legible than the simple decoration of the fourth style, in which, above the low red plinth, the panels of the white middle area are separated by compartments with candelabra. In the photograph you can see the large shards inserted in the plaster preparation layer. 79 N52676
17. Room (i), N wall, section E: remains of a fresco of the fourth style, with a red plinth adorned with a hanging garland. 79 N52726

16. Room (i), N wall, section O with rectangular splayed window. The room probably served as a triclinium, as both the location near the viridarium (1) and the decoration, which - although extremely simple - is enriched compared to the rest of the house by the presence of figures of Nymphs, which probably represented the Seasons. In the red plinth, slightly lower than usual, narrow compartments with plants alternate with panels containing garlands hanging from stylized architecture. The middle area has a white central panel (on the right in the photograph), flanked by a yellow panel and a red panel with a central medallion. The upper area has almost completely collapsed. IV style.
18. Room (i), wall E, section N: remains of a fresco of the fourth style, concluded at the top by a stucco frame.
19. Room (i), wall E, section N: detail of the stucco frame. 79 N52725

20. Room (i), S wall: remains of a fresco of the fourth style. In the upper area there are still traces of painted architecture, under which there is a previous layer, speckled by the adhesion of the fresco of the fourth style.
21. Room (i), wall O: remains of a fresco of the fourth style with an aedicule (?) in the centre on a white background and a red side panel.
21. Room (i), wall O: remains of a fresco of the fourth style with an aedicule (?) in the centre on a white background and a red side panel.

23. Fauces (k), N wall: the rear part of the room was obtained by narrowing the adjacent viridarium (1) by means of a partition, to whose decoration the remains reproduced here belong, with a middle area of black panels bordered by white and red bands. IV style.

24. Fauces (k), wall E, section N: this wall also originally belonged to the viridarium (1), of which this black panel is part of the original decoration, crossed horizontally by a garland ' on which a bird rests. IV style. 79 N52689
25. Fauces (k), wall E, section S: in the front part of the room the decoration consists of a high plinth, in which red panels alternate with narrow yellow compartments. IV style.
26. Fauces (k), wall O, section S: compartment with a yellow background crossed by a twisted candelabrum between red panels. IV style.  79 N52700
27. Fauces(k), O face, S section: bird in flight in the centre of the high red panel of the hoof. IV style. 79 N52703
28. Viridarium (1), NE corner: drainage channels lined with cocciopesto. 79 N52690

29. Viridarium (1), N wall: the room has a simple decoration with a low black plinth with yellow splashes and panels with plants. The middle area is also black and contains panels separated by narrow compartments crossed by gilded candelabras. Above, the wall is covered with rough plaster, under which the remains of an older decoration are visible.
30. Viridarium (1), N wall, section E: traces of the decoration in the centre of the black panel, consisting of a bird resting on an arched garland. IV style.

31. Viridarium (1), wall E, with windows and the door open to the jaws (k). The construction of the wall, covered with simple rough plaster, is related to a modification of the environment, on the occasion of which even a column of the portico was incorporated into the masonry.

32. Viridarium (1), O wall: low black plinth with simple yellow splashes, divided into pan-. nelli with plants; high middle area with black panels separated by compartments with candelabras; upper area with rough plaster. The decoration, dating back to the fourth style, has almost completely collapsed. In front of the wall a dolio in fragments is driven into the ground.
33. Viridarium (1), wall O, section N: the only decorative motif still preserved consists of an arched garland that crosses the panel with a black background in the middle area. IV style.
34. Room (m): section of floor in cocciopesto plastered red.

35. Room (m), wall N: in this room, as elsewhere in the house, the very simple decoration is based on a two-part scheme. In the plinth, the red plaster has almost completely collapsed; The white middle area has a large compartment crossed by a candelabra in the center and two panels squared by simple stretched garlands on the sides. Above the upper area, almost completely collapsed, are the remains of the molded stucco cornice. IV style.
36. Room (m), wall E: remains of a fresco of the fourth style.
37. Room (m), S wall: traces of a panel with plants are preserved in the red plinth. IV style.

38. Cubicle (n), wall N: this room, like all the others in the house, has a very simple decoration, more frequent in work environments than in living rooms, consisting of a high red plinth with panels above which is the white middle area. The lack of decorative details makes it difficult to propose a date, but it is to be assumed that the room was decorated in the same phase in which, in the rest of the house, the paintings of the fourth style were executed.
39. Cubicle (n), wall E with high plinth with red panels.

40. Cubicle (n), S wall with built-in bed. The space in the small room is further reduced by the presence of a staircase, whose position is highlighted by the course of the plaster. Above the high red paneled plinth, the middle area is white.
41. Cubicle (0): remains of the cocciopesto floor. 79 N52710

42. Cubicle (o), N wall with high recess for the bed. This is the best preserved room in the house, whose decoration consists of a red paneled plinth, surmounted by a middle area and a white upper area. At the top there are remains of an older stucco frame.
43. Cubicle (o), N wall, section O: detail of the stucco frame with palmettes and trefoils, on which the plaster of the upper area, more recent (at this point almost completely collapsed) rests.
44. Cubicle (0), N wall, central section: on the upper white area you can barely read the traces of a shrine, on a corner of which a bird is perched. IV style.

45. Cubicle (0), N wall, section E: inside the recess for the bed, the fourth style decoration continues, consisting of a red panelled plinth with plants separated by narrow compartments and a white middle area.

47. Cubicle (o), wall E with lunette; The loss of the background colour reveals some details of the decoration: in the centre of the white middle area is a large candelabrum, in the side panels vignettes with birds (see fig. below); in the upper white area there are light architectures between which garlands hang. A stucco frame divides the wall decoration from the lunette (in turn concluded by a stucco frame), in which there was a still life with a peacock and a head of fruit. At the top of the photograph is visible, under the plaster just described, an older plaster belonging to the same phase in which the stucco frames were made, tapped to better adhere to the more recent plaster, of the IV style.
46. Cubicle (o), N wall, section E: detail of the simple stretched garland that delimits the white panel of the middle area. IV style.
48. Cubicle (o), wall E, section N: in the centre of the panel are barely visible the remains of a very simple decorative motif, consisting of a vignette with a bird. IV style.
49. Cubicle (o), wall E, section N: detail of the stucco, lotus and pelte cornices, belonging to the oldest phase of decoration of the room.
50. Room (0), wall E, section N: the stucco frames with astragals and lotuses and palmettes that delimit the lunette.

51. Room (o), S wall: the decoration is based on that preserved on the wall in front (see fig. 42). The large hole at the left end of the photograph, filled in by the restoration, is the trace of the passage into the environment of ancient prospectors, who returned to the site after the eruption of 79 AD.
52. Room (o), S wall, section E: in the centre of the panel was a vignette with a bird, now completely eva-nida. IV style.
53. Room (w), S wall: traces of the twisted candelabrum that marked the centre of the decoration are barely visible. IV style.
54. Room (0), S wall, section O: detail of the IV style decoration, superimposed on an older fresco, contemporary with the stucco frame with tongues.

55. Room (0), wall O: plinth with red panels; z0na white median adorned with panels with vignettes; white upper area with architecture. The fall of the plaster of the fourth style reveals an underlying decoration in correspondence with the lunette, interrupted by a small rectangular splayed window.
56. Room (W), wall W, section N: in the centre of the panel is a vignette with a pecking bird. IV style.

57. Room (o'), wall W with square window. The room, which is located above room (o), also has a decoration of the fourth style consisting of a red plinth and a white middle area, in the center of which is a narrow compartment with a twisted candelabrum, flanked by panels with carpet edges. IV style. 79 N52728
2. The façade of the house in an old photograph.

1. The façade of the house, on the Via degli Augustali, preserves above the masonry in opus incerta, the traces of the decorative apparatus of the Republican age: the portal, high and narrow, is flanked by two pilasters covered with stucco, which end with tuff capitals, simply squared; the masonry in opus incerta is covered with rows of ashlars made in stucco relief. This cladding, dating back to the Republican age, has been partly renovated in correspondence with the middle area.
3. Detail of the façade; The pilasters were chiseled at the base for the insertion of a Palombino threshold.

4. Vestibule (a), wall E: even the tall and narrow fauces preserve in the upper area three rows of carefully executed ashlars (originally yellow, red and green), which were later restored with a layer of rough plaster. The vestibule opened onto the atrium by means of two stucco-covered pilasters, partially preserved. I style. 79 N52756
5. Vestibule (a), wall O, with stucco cladding of the first style partially renovated by a layer of rough plaster.

6. Atrium (d): view of the table 7. Atrium (d): edge of the pan (m) with the opening of the floor in the risastibulo papier-mâché (a) flanked by the lenses of the Republican age and the doors of the cubicles (c) and (b).

6. Atrium (d): view of the table 7. Atrium (d): edge of the pan (m) with the opening of the floor in the risastibulo papier-mâché (a) flanked by the lenses of the Republican age and the doors of the cubicles (c) and (b).

8. Atrium (d): detail of the papier-mâché floor, soberly illuminated by the insertion of white tiles of different sizes and fragments of colored glass (blue, yellow, red and green, according to Pernice, cited in the bibl.). This flooring also dates back to the decorative phase of the first style.

9. Atrium (d), corner S-0: an oven is leaning against the masonry. The walls of the room are covered with two layers of plaster, one of which, according to Mau's testimony (cited in the bibl.), dates back to the second style. On the left of the photograph are visible the limestone blocks that make up the jamb of the cubicle door (b).
11. Atrium (d): mouth of a square travertine cistern, on the S side of the impluvium, which was covered with cocciopesto.  79 N52777
10. Atrium (d), N side, section to the E of the tablinum door (m): a high plinth, ending in an upper red area and datable to the II style (cf. Mau, cited in bibl.), covers the jamb in brick curtain.
12. Atrium (d): smooth travertine support, which supported a smooth table top of the same material (Pernice T, p. 8). 79 N52785
13. Cubicle (b): the rest of the cocciopesto floor, in which large white limestone tiles were scattered.

14. Cubicle (b), N wall with the door open to the atrium (d). The state of conservation requires a reconstructive effort to imagine the original appearance of the typical room of the Republican age, divided into a lower part, intended for the bed and covered by a false vault (alcove) and in a front part (antechamber), also covered by a false vault, at the entrance to the room. A red pilaster marked the distinction between antechamber and alcove. The oldest wall covering has been preserved in the upper area, subject to less wear, and has instead been restored in correspondence with the lower part of the wall (plinth and middle area).

15. Cubicle (b), NW corner: remains of the protruding stucco frames belonging to the first style cladding of the alcove. The area between the two frames appears to be devoid of the last layer of stucco finishing.
16. Cubicle (b), N wall,
17. Cubicle (b), N wall, section O: above the lunette, finished with a simple moulded frame, the holes in the beams that supported the reed of the false vaulted ceiling are visible.

18. Cubicle (b), wall E: the antechamber preserves only in the upper area the remains of stucco frames of the first style, while the lower part of the wall, more exposed to wear, has been restored with a simple plaster covering mixed with cocciopesto.

19. Cubicle (b), wall S: the conservation conditions of the room do not allow us to distinguish the decoration of the antechamber (on the left of the photograph; it was covered by a false vaulted ceiling) from that of the alcove (also covered by a false vaulted ceiling, but located at a lower level). Also on this wall, as on the N wall, a pilaster will have marked the separation between the antechamber and the alcove. The plinth and middle area have been restored with cocciopesto and plaster.
20. Cubicle (b), wall W of the alcove: plinth and middle area restored with cocciopesto mixed with plaster, and original stucco cornices in the upper area.

21. Cubicle (c): the cubicle in a symmetrical position to the previous one also retains remains of the decoration of the first style (see fig. below), while the plinth and the middle area have been renewed by a decoration with a red background that can be assigned to the fourth style and datable to the last phase of Pompeii.
23. Cubicle (c): remains of the restoration in cocciopesto and rough plaster on the W wall of the room, which originally had a first-style cladding.  79 N52782

22. Cubicle (c), S wall: in the splay of the window open on the Via degli Augustali the remains of the original decoration of the first style are visible, covered instead by a layer of cocciopesto in the plinth and plaster in the middle area.
24. Cubicle (f): view from the W with recess for the bed in the N wall and remains of frescoes.
25. Room (i), S wall with the remains of frescoes now illegible.

26. Wing (k), wall N: the decoration of the last phase of the room, which can be assigned to the IV style, is very simple and consists of a plinth and a middle area, both with a white background, with panels bordered by red bands.
27. Wing (k), S wall: below the IV style decoration on a white background there was another one (barely visible in the photograph), on a black background.

28. Wing (k): the O wall retains larger passages of the penultimate decorative phase of the room, which consists of a black plinth, surmounted by a middle area with a central aedicule (?) also with a black background and red side panels.

29. Tablinum (m): the cocciopesto floor, partly restored in ancient times but originally painted red, is assigned by Pernice (cited in the bibl.) to the decorative phase of the Republican age (I style).

30. Tablinum (m), wall E, decoration in a two-part scheme: on the sides of a central compartment that contained a twisted candelabrum (typical motif of the IV style) are two panels with a yellow background.
31. Tablinum (m), S wall, section E: detail of the edges of a triangle carpet (also a typical motif of the IV style) that delimit the yellow side panel.
32. Tablinum (m), wall O: remains of a fresco of the fourth style with a central compartment containing a candelabrum and yellow side panels.

33. Triclinium (n): according to Pernice (cited in the bibl.), the cocciopesto floor retained part of a black and white tesserae decoration and was assignable to the first style, and therefore to the decorative phase of the house datable to the Republican age. 79 N52753

34. Triclinium (n), wall N: in the middle area we can now read very thin traces of the fresco, which simulated a covering of marble slabs typical of the II style, a phase to which Mau (cited in bibl.) assigned the decoration of this room.
35. Triclinium (n), wall E with remains of a fresco of the second style.

36. Triclinium (n), wall W: above the recess for the bed (which perhaps dates back to a modification of the room) the remains of the decoration of the second style (I century BC) are also preserved on this wall.
37. Peristyle (0), seen from the E with brick columns that preserve remains of plaster: in the foreground are a millstone and a cistern mouth, both in lava.

38. Room (p), wall E: the room, open to the peristyle (o), retains traces of a very simple covering (and frequent in rooms intended for carrying out production activities), consisting of a high white plinth, on which the panels are indicated by red bands, and an upper area of rough plaster. The room had previously received a different covering, of which very few remains are preserved (visible at the corners of the wall, in the upper area of the photograph).
39. Room (p), wall E, section N: remains of the oldest decoration attested in the room.
40. Room (p), wall E, section S: remains of the oldest decoration preserved in the room.
41. Room (q): above the uncertain masonry of wall E only the remains of a decoration with a red background are preserved. 79 N52767
42. Room (q), S wall with remains of a fresco on a red background.

43. Kitchen (s), oven on the N. side A narrow corridor leads from the living rooms into this room, equipped with an oven with the im. mouthpiece protected by an arch with brick cladding. On the side of the oven there is another work area on the left. In the foreground is the vaulted room that further protects the cooking area. '79 N52766
44. Kitchen(s): counter with brick-covered top leaning against the wall E. 79 N52765

1. The large workshop (p) preserves on the wall E the remains of the red plinth and, rather at the top, the small lararium niche covered with white plaster. The quadrangular holes attest to the position of a mezzanine right above the entrance.

2-3. A clear sign of a previous different use of this room is the large Doric column of tuff, incorporated into the masonry of the partition wall that separates the faux (b) from the basement (c). Along the W wall there are five cylindrical dolii and near the entrance there is a travertine mortar. '79 N60122 - 79 N60166

2-3. A clear sign of a previous different use of this room is the large Doric column of tuff, incorporated into the masonry of the partition wall that separates the faux (b) from the basement (c). Along the W wall there are five cylindrical dolii and near the entrance there is a travertine mortar. '79 N60122 - 79 N60166
1. Shop 4: the serving counter, of which only the N-W corner is preserved, contained three dolii today (1996) recognizable only by the bases still underground.

2. Cubicle (e): located next to the tablinum (d), the small cubicle had large walls in opus incerta with limestone block doors resting on the travertine threshold in which the housing for the wooden jambs are hollowed. The cubicle (e) overlooked the small atrium (b), (not visible in the photograph), with a quadrangular impluvium covered with marble. 79 N60171

3. Cubicle (e): the cocciopesto floor with irregular flakes of green and white limestone scattered dates back to the end of the second century BC, a period to which the primitive layout of the house can be traced.

4. Cubicle (e): the decoration carried out in the fourth style is extremely simple; the plinth is red, the white middle area without vertical partitions is enriched only by the stucco frame with a top surmounted by the lotus and trefoil motif; the upper area has rough plaster.
5. Cubicle (e): the wall O has the recess for the bed in which the same simple decoration continues as the rest of the wall.

6. Triclinium (d): located in the S-E corner of the lot occupied by the house, the residential environment had a large window open towards the viridarium (i) in such a position, however, as to have only a glimpse of the view of the aedicule flanked by niches with candelabra. The walls had a red plinth and a white middle area. The attitude of the god, standing and in an upright position, although the right leg is crossed in front of the left, with the caduceus raised, the left resting on the side, contrasts with the abandonment of Venus who, as usual, seems concentrated in the ostentation of her own beauty. The central element, a column at the base of which is an ithyphallic Priapus with a palm branch in his left hand and which is decorated at the top with a crown, has not helped exegetes in the interpretation of the scene that according to some could represent Venus at the tomb of Adonis, according to others Mercury forcing Calypso to let Odysseus go,  and which probably, as proposed by Helbig and generally accepted, is simply the depiction of two deities obtained by combining models not necessarily united in an original cartoon. It should be noted that Venus is the tutelary deity of the Colonia Cornelia Veneria Pompeianorum and that Mercury is the protector of commercial activities and traffic, so it is not strange to find him protecting shops.

68. Oecus (24), W wall, central panel with Dionysus and Ariadne: drawing by N.La Volpe executed in situ before the panel was detached and transferred to Naples. La Volpe's etching is the most reliable of the various nineteenth-century reproductions of this famous painting, to which the house owes one of its names. Ariadne lies asleep on a small rocky terrace. She wears a bracelet on each arm and wears a chiton that covers only her legs; she leans on the right leg of a winged male figure sitting behind her. The latter has a crown, wears boots and wears a cloak falling from the shoulder on the right arm. In his left hand he holds a phiàle, in his right a branch. Next to him is a standing cupid who lifts a corner of Ariadne's cloak and draws Dionysus' gaze to his splendid discovery. The god, at the head of his thyasos, is depicted in the center of the painting; he wears only a small cloak and boots, wears a crown on his hair, grasps the thyrsus with his right hand and seizes a Maenad that stands on his left. This figure also wears a crown and has a thyrsus in his left hand. Two other Maenads, represented in the background, are part of the god's retinue; one of them seems to be looking at Ariadne, while the second is arguing animatedly with one of her companions, towards whom she extends her right hand in an unfriendly gesture. The Satyr in question is seen from the back, partly cut from the frame of the painting; he wears a short cloak and wears thyrsus resting on his right shoulder. The heads of three other Satyrs appear behind the two quarrelling, while in front of them is an old Silenus, bald and with a white beard; He wears a short cloak that, slipped from his shoulders, covers only his legs, as he tries to climb the steep slope of the hill. With his left hand he leans on a staff, assisted by a younger Satyr who reaches forward to grab the Silenus' right arm with both hands. This one is also naked, apart from an animal skin loincloth; The crown on his head seems to be made of pine needles. The background is divided into two almost equal halves by the wall of a building from whose window a tree emerges. On the right there are some rocks and a structure of INS. 4, 31.51

103. Tablinum (27), wall O, decoration in IV style; watercolour by A. Magliano published by F. Niccolini, (see fig. 102). The few elements visible in situ confirm that, apart from a few secondary details, Magliano's drawing illustrates the wall accurately. White background except in the plinth (red); the latter is divided into three fields by two blue frames, inside which are garlanded swans flying towards the center of the wall. Each of the three fields has a head in the center, inside a circle flanked by two large borders with yellow palmettes, in the central field, and a square in the two lateral fields. Each square is framed by horizontal garlands and floral borders. The latter connect the three emblems to the cornet above and to the white base line. The main element of the middle area is represented by two symmetrical views, framed by slender candelabra, with fantastic architecture in perspective flanked by high pedestals, on top of each of which is probably a bronze or gold goat statue; steps lead to an open door. A garland hangs from its architrave in front of two slender pillars that support an arched entablature and close the lower part of the foreshortening. On a second level there is an elegant balcony supported by two volute shelves. Two birds sit on the central balustrade, while the side railings support two pillars. Two sphinxes are represented at the top of the projecting entablatures. At the top of the foreshortening there is a coffered ceiling with an opening similar to an impluvium, bordered by antefixes.

Marsigli, now in the Museo Naz. of Naples (ADS 621; see also Disegnatori, p.205, fig. 90). A comparison with two other reproductions of the same painting, one by N. The Fox (MB XI, fig. 35; source by RP, p. 111, 6), the other by S. Mastracchio (Naples, Museo Naz., ADS 622; see also Disegnatori, p. 833, fig. 12), and with Helbig's description (H, 1234), suggests that Roux's reproduction is quite accurate. Arianna sits in the foreground on a blue mattress resting on the flat and sandy ground. He has his right leg crossed on his left and rests on his left arm, behind which is a large blue cushion. With bracelets on both wrists and a band in her hair, she turns her gaze to the sea, in the upper left corner of the painting, where Theseus' boat is about to set sail, with its sail inflated by the wind. She wears a cloak that covers only her legs, leaving her feet and upper body bare; he lifts a flap to dry his tears. She is not aware of the arrival of Dionysus and his retinue: the god, wearing an ivy garland and a purple cloak covering his back and legs, is depicted standing and frontal behind her, with the thyrsus in his left hand lowered, and with his right hand on the shoulder of a Silenus with a white beard,  represented on the right. The latter seems naked, however his legs are hidden by the figure of Ariadne. He holds a thyrsus in his right hand, but the garland that crowns his head is of vines. Between the heads of Dionysus and Silenus is the face of a Maenad standing in the background. Like her companion, depicted behind the god's left arm, in a long green robe, she wears a garland of pine needles on her hair. Between the Silenus and the sea, on the left, a rock rises to the top of the painting.
